title: Statement and Assumption
summary: What counts as an implicit assumption, the negation test that decides it, and the four quick checks that reject a stated fact, an over-strong claim, an unconnected idea, or a mere hope.
learningObjectives: Define an implicit assumption as an unstated idea the statement depends on.
Apply the negation test: if denying it breaks the statement, it is assumed.
Reject an option that merely restates the statement or is unconnected to it.
Reject an option that is stronger or wider than the statement needs.

blocks.title: What an assumption is
blocks.markdown:
An **assumption** is something the speaker takes for granted — not written in the statement, but needed for the statement to make sense or to have any point.

It is not the same as a conclusion (which *follows from* the statement) or an inference (which *may* follow). An assumption sits *underneath* the statement and holds it up.

A typical item gives a statement and two candidate assumptions, I and II, and asks which are 'implicit' — that is, genuinely relied on.

not a conclusion not an inference sits underneath
which assumptions are implicit

blocks.title: The negation test
blocks.markdown:
The single most reliable check:

1. **Write the opposite of the candidate assumption.**
2. **Put that opposite next to the statement.**
3. **If the statement now falls apart** — becomes pointless, impossible, or self-defeating — the assumption is implicit.
4. **If the statement still stands** with the opposite true, the assumption is not implicit.

Statement: *'Use the mobile app for balance checks to cut counter queues.'* Candidate: *'Some customers have phones that can run the app.'* Negate it: *no customer has such a phone*. Then the advice helps no one — the statement collapses. So the assumption is implicit.
searchKeywords: negation test write the opposite put it next to the statement
if the statement falls apart the assumption is implicit

blocks.title: Four quick rejections
blocks.markdown:
Before the negation test, an option can often be dismissed outright:

- **Already stated.** If it just repeats part of the statement, it is not an *unstated* assumption.
- **Too strong or too wide.** Words like *all*, *every*, *never*, *only*, *always* usually overreach what the statement needs.
- **Not connected.** If it talks about cost, history, or motive that the statement does not lean on, it is out.
- **A hope, not a basis.** *'People will respond well'* is a desired outcome, not something the statement takes for granted.
searchKeywords: quick rejections already stated too strong too wide all every never
not connected cost history motive
a hope not a basis desired outcome

blocks.title: Notices, appeals and instructions
blocks.markdown:
Many items are worded as a notice or an instruction. Two assumptions are almost always in play:

- **The audience can act on it.** A notice telling staff to use the stairs assumes there *are* usable stairs.
- **The audience will see it.** An appeal assumes the people it targets will read it.

Anything beyond those — that the audience *agrees*, that the action will *succeed* — is usually a step too far and fails the negation test.
searchKeywords: notices appeals instructions audience can act on it can see it
stairs notice assumes usable stairs appeal assumes people read it
agreement or success is a step too far

blocks.title: Worked examples
blocks.markdown:
**1.** Statement: *'To cut queueing, the bank has asked customers to use the mobile app for balance checks.'*

- I. A number of customers own phones that can run the app. Negate: none do. Then the request cannot cut queues. **Implicit.**
- II. Balance checks make up a meaningful share of counter visits. Negate: they are negligible. Then moving them would not affect queues, and the statement's purpose fails. **Implicit.**

Both I and II are implicit.

**2.** Statement: *'Notice: the lift will be shut for repair on Sunday; staff should use the stairs.'*

- I. The building has stairs that staff can use. Negate: it has none. Then the instruction is impossible. **Implicit.**
- II. The lift cannot be repaired while it is running. Negate: it can. The notice does not depend on this — it is about Sunday access, not repair method. **Not implicit.**

Only I is implicit.
searchKeywords: worked example bank mobile app balance checks both implicit
lift shut sunday use the stairs only I implicit

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.markdown:
- **Marking an assumption implicit because it is true in the real world.** It must be something *this statement* relies on, not just a fact.
- **Accepting an option with *all* or *every*** when the statement only needs *some*.
- **Treating a restated part of the statement as an assumption.**
- **Rejecting a plainly needed assumption** because it 'feels too obvious' — obvious ones are still implicit.
- **Bringing in cost, history, or intent** the statement never uses.
- **Skipping the negation test** and going on gut feel.
searchKeywords: assumption mistakes true in the real world all every when some suffices
restated part obvious ones still implicit
cost history intent skipping the negation test

blocks.title: Quick revision
blocks.markdown:
- An assumption is unstated and load-bearing: the statement needs it.
- Negation test: deny the candidate; if the statement then collapses, the assumption is implicit; if the statement survives, it is not.
- Quick rejects: already stated, too strong or wide (*all*, *never*), unconnected, or a mere hope.
- Notice and appeal items almost always assume the audience can act on the message and will see it — but not that they will agree or that it will work.
searchKeywords: statement assumption summary revision negation test
quick rejects already stated too strong unconnected a hope
notice appeal audience can act and will see

blocks.title: Practice
blocks.markdown:
For each, mark I, II, both, or neither as implicit, and give a one-line negation-test reason.

1. Statement: *'Submit the form by Friday so it can be processed next week.'*  I. Forms received after Friday cannot be processed next week.  II. The office will be working next week.
2. Statement: *'Our new branch has extended hours to serve working customers better.'*  I. Some working customers find the standard hours inconvenient.  II. Every customer of the branch is employed.
3. Statement: *'The training was moved online to reach staff in remote branches.'*  I. Remote-branch staff have a way to access online training.  II. Online training costs the bank less than in-person training.
4. Statement: *'Warning: never share your OTP with anyone, including bank staff.'*  I. Bank staff do not need a customer's OTP to do their work.  II. Customers sometimes receive requests to share their OTP.
5. Statement: *'Switch off your monitor before leaving to save electricity.'*  I. A monitor left on consumes electricity.  II. All staff leave the office at the same time.
6. Statement: *'The bank has added a ramp at the entrance.'*  I. Some visitors to the bank cannot use steps.  II. The entrance previously had a step or a level change.
7. Statement: *'Apply online; postal applications will not be accepted this year.'*  I. Applicants have a means to apply online.  II. Postal applications were accepted in earlier years.

flashcards.front: What is an implicit assumption in these questions?
flashcards.back: An idea not written in the statement that the statement nonetheless depends on — it sits underneath the statement and holds it up.
flashcards.explanation: Different from a conclusion, which follows from the statement.

flashcards.front: State the negation test for an assumption.
flashcards.back: Negate the candidate assumption and place it beside the statement. If the statement then falls apart, the assumption is implicit; if the statement still stands, it is not.

flashcards.front: An option says 'every customer of the branch is employed'. Why is it usually not implicit?
flashcards.back: It is far stronger than the statement needs. The statement only needs that *some* customers work; 'every' overreaches.
flashcards.explanation: Watch for all / every / never / only / always.

flashcards.front: An assumption option is a true real-world fact. Does that make it implicit?
flashcards.back: No. It is implicit only if this particular statement relies on it. A true but unused fact fails the negation test.
flashcards.explanation: Relevance to the statement, not truth, is the test.

flashcards.front: Which two assumptions almost always underlie a notice or an appeal?
flashcards.back: That the audience can act on the message (the means exist) and that the audience will see it.
flashcards.explanation: Agreement or success is usually a step too far.

flashcards.front: An option repeats part of the statement almost word for word. Implicit or not?
flashcards.back: Not implicit. An assumption must be unstated. A restatement of the statement is not an assumption.
flashcards.explanation: Quick reject before the negation test.

flashcards.front: Is 'people will respond well to this' typically an implicit assumption?
flashcards.back: No. It is a hoped-for outcome, not something the statement takes for granted. It fails the negation test.
flashcards.explanation: Desired results are conclusions at best, not assumptions.
